title: Given a Scenario, Use Data Sources to Support an Investigation

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: An investigation is built from evidence. Analysts use multiple data sources to determine what happened, when it happened, which systems were involved, who or what initiated the activity, and how far the incident spread.
Objective 4.9 asks you to start with the investigation question, choose the source most likely to record the needed evidence, and correlate multiple sources into a reliable timeline.

entries.title: Investigation Decision Pattern
paragraphs: Define the exact evidence needed, select the source that records it most directly, and then correlate supporting sources to confirm the sequence of events.
entries.recognitionCue: Question -> correct data source -> correlated evidence -> incident timeline

sections.callout: One data source rarely tells the whole story.

sections.title: Data Sources and Log Data
paragraphs: Investigation evidence can come from security controls, systems, applications, endpoints, network infrastructure, scans, reports, dashboards, and captured traffic.

entries.title: Data Sources
paragraphs: Data sources are the broader evidence inputs used to answer investigation questions. Each source has a different viewpoint, so investigators choose sources according to the facts they need.
entries.recognitionCue: Evidence inputs used to support an investigation -> Data sources

entries.title: Log Data
paragraphs: A log records events generated by a system, application, device, or security control. Different logs answer different questions about network, application, endpoint, identity, and infrastructure activity.
entries.recognitionCue: Recorded event information used during an investigation -> Log data

sections.title: Firewall Logs
paragraphs: Firewall records are the direct source for determining how a firewall handled traffic.

entries.title: Firewall Logs
paragraphs: Firewall logs can record source and destination addresses, ports, protocols, rules, and whether a connection was allowed, denied, or translated.
entries.recognitionCue: Was network traffic permitted or denied? -> Firewall log

sections.title: Application and Endpoint Logs
paragraphs: Application logs describe activity inside a specific program, while endpoint logs describe activity occurring on an individual workstation, laptop, or server.

entries.title: Application Logs
paragraphs: Application logs record application-specific login activity, errors, transactions, requests, and other events produced by the software.
entries.recognitionCue: What happened inside the application? -> Application log

entries.title: Endpoint Logs
paragraphs: Endpoint logs can reveal processes, file activity, malware alerts, and endpoint-security events on workstations and servers.
entries.recognitionCue: What process, file, or security activity occurred on this device? -> Endpoint log

table.caption: Application and endpoint evidence
rows: Events produced by a specific application
Processes, files, and security activity on a device

sections.title: OS-Specific Security Logs
paragraphs: Operating systems maintain security-focused audit records that are especially useful for identity and privilege questions.

entries.title: OS-Specific Security Logs
paragraphs: OS-specific security logs record authentication, account changes, authorization, privilege use, and operating-system security policy events.
entries.recognitionCue: Which account authenticated or used privileges in the operating system? -> OS-specific security log

sections.title: IPS/IDS Logs
paragraphs: Intrusion detection and prevention systems record suspicious patterns observed in network traffic.

entries.title: IPS/IDS Logs
paragraphs: IPS/IDS logs may record triggered signatures, detected attacks, source and destination information, alert details, and any blocking action.
entries.recognitionCue: Which suspicious network pattern or attack signature fired? -> IPS/IDS log

sections.title: Network Logs
paragraphs: Network infrastructure creates records that help investigators understand communications and device events across the environment.

entries.title: Network Logs
paragraphs: Network logs can come from routers, switches, wireless devices, and network services. They summarize infrastructure activity rather than preserving every packet.
entries.recognitionCue: What happened on network infrastructure? -> Network log

sections.title: Metadata
paragraphs: Metadata describes other data and can help place files, communications, and events into context.

entries.title: Metadata
paragraphs: Metadata can include timestamps, ownership, creation and modification dates, source and destination information, and file size.
entries.memoryHook: Metadata is data about the data.
entries.recognitionCue: When was this file created or modified, and who owns it? -> Metadata

sections.title: Vulnerability Scans
paragraphs: An investigation may need to determine whether an affected system already had a known weakness that could have been exploited.

entries.title: Vulnerability Scans
paragraphs: Vulnerability scan results identify known weaknesses, insecure configurations, affected assets, and other exposure information that can help explain how a compromise became possible.
entries.recognitionCue: Did the system have a known weakness or insecure configuration? -> Vulnerability scan

sections.title: Automated Reports and Dashboards
paragraphs: Both tools summarize security information, but they present it for different uses.

entries.title: Automated Reports
paragraphs: Automated reports are system-generated summaries of alert activity, vulnerability status, compliance results, trends, or other security conditions. They are often prepared for review or distribution.
entries.recognitionCue: Automatically generated security summary -> Automated report

entries.title: Dashboards
paragraphs: Dashboards visually present alert counts, trends, system health, vulnerabilities, and incident status for quick operational awareness.
entries.recognitionCue: Visual current-state overview of security data -> Dashboard

table.caption: Automated reports and dashboards
rows: Generated summary for review or distribution
Visual current-state view used for monitoring

sections.title: Packet Captures
paragraphs: A packet capture preserves network packets for detailed examination rather than only summarizing network events.

entries.title: Packet Captures
paragraphs: Packet captures may expose source and destination information, protocols, headers, sessions, and payload data when the payload is visible.
entries.memoryHook: A network log is a record of the conversation; a packet capture is a recording of the conversation.
entries.recognitionCue: What actually crossed the network? -> Packet capture

table.caption: Network log and packet capture
rows: A recorded summary of network or infrastructure events

sections.title: Choosing the Correct Data Source
paragraphs: Several sources may contain useful information, but the strongest answer is usually the source that provides the most direct evidence for the stated question.

table.caption: Investigation questions and direct evidence sources
rows: Was the connection allowed or blocked?
Which account authenticated to the operating system?
Did the endpoint launch a suspicious process?
Did a known attack signature fire?
Was the server vulnerable before compromise?

sections.callout: Choose the source based on the evidence you need, not simply the tool with the most data.

sections.title: Correlating Data Sources
paragraphs: Investigations often combine network, host, identity, and application evidence. A firewall log may show an allowed connection, an IDS log may identify an attack signature, an endpoint log may show a suspicious process, and an OS security log may identify the account used.
Correlating timestamps and related evidence across these sources builds a stronger incident timeline than relying on any single source.
sections.callout: Network evidence + host evidence + identity evidence -> incident timeline

sections.title: Recognition Cues
paragraphs: Ask what exact fact the investigation needs, then select the source that records it most directly.
bullets: Allowed or blocked connection -> Firewall log
Application-specific event -> Application log
Process or file activity on a device -> Endpoint log
Operating-system login or privilege event -> OS-specific security log
Attack signature or suspicious network pattern -> IPS/IDS log
Network-infrastructure event -> Network log
Data describing data -> Metadata
Known weakness or insecure configuration -> Vulnerability scan
Generated security summary -> Automated report
Visual operational overview -> Dashboard
Actual captured network traffic -> Packet capture

sections.title: Objective 4.9 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Firewall logs show whether traffic was allowed or blocked; IPS/IDS logs show suspicious or malicious patterns and triggered detection logic.
Endpoint logs show broader host activity such as processes and files; OS-specific security logs focus on operating-system authentication, authorization, and security events.
Network logs summarize recorded events; packet captures preserve detailed packets.
Dashboards provide a visual operational view; automated reports provide generated summaries.
Vulnerability scans show weaknesses that could be exploited; IDS alerts show suspicious activity that actually occurred or matched detection logic.
sections.callout: Ask: What exact piece of evidence do I need? Then choose the source that records it most directly.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
paragraphs: Keep these final pairings ready for fast recognition.
bullets: Allowed or blocked? -> Firewall log; application did what? -> Application log
Endpoint process or file activity? -> Endpoint log
OS login or security event? -> OS-specific security log
Attack signature fired? -> IPS/IDS log
Network infrastructure event? -> Network log
Data about data? -> Metadata
Was the system vulnerable? -> Vulnerability scan
Generated summary? -> Automated report; visual overview? -> Dashboard
What crossed the wire? -> Packet capture
Several clues tell one story -> Correlate data sources

miniCheck.intro: Choose the most direct data source for each investigation question.
miniCheck.prompt: An analyst must first determine whether the edge firewall allowed an outbound connection to a suspicious address. The analyst must then examine the exact network packets exchanged during that session.

fields.label: Most direct source for determining whether the firewall allowed the connection
Most direct source for examining the exact packets exchanged

miniCheck.correctFeedback: Correct. The firewall log records whether the connection was permitted or denied, while the packet capture contains the detailed packets exchanged during the session.
miniCheck.retryFeedback: Not quite. Identify the source that records a firewall permit-or-deny decision, then identify the source that preserves the actual packets. Review Firewall Logs and Packet Captures and try again.
